newsitem.title: JAPAN: Mazda seen steering out of red but future bumpy.
newsitem.headline: Mazda seen steering out of red but future bumpy.

text.p: Mazda Motor Corp is likely to stay out of the red in its first earnings results since Ford's Henry Wallace slipped into the driving seat, but the road ahead still looks bumpy.

After a string of losses, Mazda is likely to at least break even for the six months to the end of September, analysts say, which should be a boost for its new president, the first foreigner to head a major Japanese firm.

Wallace took the wheel at Mazda, Japan's fifth-largest auto maker, in June soon after Ford Motor Co raised its holding in Mazda to a one-third stake from the previous 25 percent, which gave it management control.

"The effects of the new president have already emerged in the company's advertisements and dealership restructuring," said Nomura Research Institute analyst Seiji Sugiura, referring to a new ad campaign featuring Wallace himself.
But he said no major effects would be felt in car production -- such as using interchangeable parts in various models to cut costs -- until the year 2002.

Mazda, whose range has failed to excite Japanese customers at a time when its competitors are coming up with a host of popular new models, should break even, or perhaps post a modest profit in the fiscal first half after posting interim losses for three years in a row, analysts said.
It is due to release its results on Friday.

Noriyuki Matsushima, a senior analyst at Nikko Research Centre, said Mazda will meet it own forecast of nil parent current profit with the help of sales of securities holdings. Current profit is pre-tax and includes losses or gains on non-operating activities such as sales of stocks.

Nomura's Sugiura said that Mazda could post a half-year profit of about one billion yen ($9 million) to two billion yen ($18 million), depending on income from the sales of its securities holdings, but others are sceptical about this in the face of recent sluggishness in stock prices.

Mazda has made a loss in the first half for three years in a row. But on a full-year basis, it posted a current profit of 1.23 billion yen ($11 million) in 1995/96 -- the first such annual profit in three years -- thanks to the sales of securities and painful cost-cutting.
Mazda's business environment remains tough, analysts said.
In the April-September period, Mazda's car sales in Japan fell nine percent from the same period a year earlier, dragging its domestic market share to 4.5 percent from 5.3 percent.
Meanwhile, the company's car exports, which account for more than half of its total vehicle sales, grew three percent in the half-year period year-on-year.

Analysts said the weaker yen would help buoy the company's current profit for the full year by making its products more competitive abroad. A dollar rise by 1 yen translates into 3 billion yen ($27 million) of annual profits for Mazda.
Matsushima said Mazda would post a profit of 10 billion yen ($90 million) for the full year, helped by the weaker yen.
But the figure is still lower than Mazda's own profit estimate of 25 billion yen ($225 million) announced in May. The dollar on Tuesday stood at around 111 yen against 100 yen a year ago. ($=111 yen)
